name: service-activator
intent: Connect an incoming message channel to an ordinary service so that the service is invoked like a local method call and its result or exception is carried back into the messaging flow.
problem: An application owns a service that other parts of the system must reach through messaging, but the service code must not depend on the messaging API: the message has to be translated into a method invocation, the return value into a reply message, and a failure into an error path, without the service ever knowing that a channel was involved.
context: Integrators that own both a channel and a piece of application logic: a broker consumer, an in-process work queue or a request-reply channel in an enterprise integration flow, where the invoked code is ordinary local (often service-layer) code and the channel may be pushed, polled or driven by a dispatcher.
benefits: The service stays messaging-ignorant: an ordinary method on an ordinary object, callable locally and unit-testable without a broker or a channel.

Transport detail - payload and header extraction, argument conversion, reply-channel resolution, exception mapping - lives in one endpoint and is written once per service exposure instead of in every consumer.
Coupling is one-way: the endpoint knows the service, the service knows nothing about the channel, so services survive transport and middleware migrations.
The same service can be exposed over several channels or transports by attaching additional activators, with no edit to the service.
Because the endpoint terminates a flow, it composes with routing, filtering and translation upstream and inherits their guarantees (selective consumption, content-based routing, guaranteed delivery).
tradeoffs: An extra layer of indirection: a failure must be attributed to the message, to the mapping or to the service, and debugging spans both sides of the endpoint.

The plain-method-call ideal breaks as soon as the service has its own transaction, threading or exception contract; the activator then has to reproduce that discipline (join the transaction, respect thread affinity, translate error types).

Reply semantics must be invented and documented: what a void or null return means, whether a reply is mandatory, where it goes when no output channel is configured, and which exception belongs on the error or invalid-message channel.

Synchronous invocation binds message throughput to the slowest service call; scaling then needs replication (competing consumers, worker pools), which reintroduces concurrency concerns inside the service.
Dynamic, reflection-based dispatch (method chosen from message content) trades compile-time safety and tooling support for flexibility, and hides the invocation contract from the compiler.

participants.responsibility: Consumes messages from the input channel, removes the envelope, converts the payload into the service's argument types, invokes the service and marshals the result or the exception back into the flow; the only participant that knows both the messaging API and the service.
Carries the requests that must invoke the service; point-to-point (one service instance per message) or publish-subscribe, pushed or polled.
The invoked application code - an ordinary object or method, often part of a service layer - performing the work with no messaging dependency; hard-wired into the activator or selected per message.
Receives the message built from the service's return value; resolved from endpoint configuration, from the request's return address, or absent for one-way activators.
Receives failures: exceptions thrown by the service, unparsable payloads and reply-required violations, so the flow does not silently lose the work.

The transport-side driver (event-driven consumer, polling consumer, dispatcher or in-process worker loop) that delivers messages to the activator and, together with it, defines the acknowledgement boundary.

use_cases: Expose an existing service-layer method to a queue or topic without adding a broker dependency to the domain code (order received -> OrderService.place).

Request-reply over messaging: a command message carries a return address and correlation id; the activator invokes the service and sends the reply so the caller continues as if it had made a remote call.
In-process worker: a work queue (asyncio.Queue, Channel<T>, tokio mpsc, Go channel, Thread::Queue) drained by a background loop that calls an application service - the same pattern without a broker.
Event-driven microservice endpoints: a command or event message is matched by pattern to a handler method that performs the business action and returns the acknowledgement.
Terminal stage of a batch or streaming pipeline, where a domain service is invoked per record instead of business rules being embedded in the stage.
Multi-transport exposure of one service during a migration: the same business method attached to a JMS queue, an HTTP adapter and a file poller by declaring three activators.

Spring Integration makes the endpoint declarative: @ServiceActivator(inputChannel = "orders") turns a method on a Spring-managed POJO into a consumer - the framework injects the payload (or @Header values), picks the method by payload type, and sends a non-null return to the configured output-channel or the inbound replyChannel header.

Apache Camel implements the EIP directly as bean integration: a route's .to("bean:myService") binds the message Exchange to an ordinary Java bean method, so the same service stays callable both from routes and by local callers.

NestJS microservices: a controller method decorated with @MessagePattern receives only the message payload over the transport (TCP, Redis, NATS, RabbitMQ) and its return value is sent back automatically as the reply; @EventPattern is the fire-and-forget variant of the same endpoint.
avoid_when: The service must itself control the messaging (selective consumption, correlation across several channels, multi-step conversations): use a message dispatcher or a process manager instead, or put an explicit consumer inside the service.
The requirement is one-way outbound publishing from the application: that is a messaging gateway or an outbound channel adapter, not an activator.

The framework in use already ships the endpoint (Spring Integration @ServiceActivator, NestJS @MessagePattern, ServiceBusProcessor, Pekko actor receive): declare the endpoint rather than rebuilding its dispatch machinery.

A plain synchronous call (local method, HTTP, gRPC) is available and acceptable: wrapping it in a channel adds broker latency, acknowledgement obligations and a new failure mode without gaining decoupling.
The invoked code is itself a messaging-aware consumer that manages its own session or transaction; the extra adapter layer is then pure indirection.
anti_patterns: Domain logic inside the activator (validation, branching, orchestration) so the ordinary service no longer exists and the messaging coupling simply moved into the handler.
Swallowing service exceptions, or acknowledging before the service transaction commits, so failures look like success and the message is lost without reaching an error or invalid-message channel.
Reflection-only dispatch with no fallback, so a malformed or unknown message aborts the endpoint instead of being routed to the invalid-message channel.
Creating an activator, or resolving the service from a container, once per message - turning an endpoint into per-message allocation and re-initialisation.
Unbounded per-message concurrency: spawning a task, thread or goroutine per message with no limit, so a slow service turns the activator into a resource-exhaustion device.
design_principles: Inversion of control: the messaging layer calls the service; the service never calls the messaging layer.
Separation of concerns: message handling (transport, headers, acknowledgement) versus business logic.
Single responsibility: the activator maps messages to method calls and results to messages, and does nothing else.
Dependency inversion: the endpoint depends on an abstract service interface and the channel abstraction, not on a concrete broker.
Open/closed: exposing another service or another transport means declaring another endpoint, not editing existing ones.
Information hiding: headers and transport metadata stay on the endpoint's side of the boundary; the service sees arguments.
best_practices: Keep the activator thin: payload extraction and result/exception mapping only; push everything else into the service.
Invoke the service with typed payload arguments rather than the framework's message type, so the service API does not inherit the messaging API.
Define the reply contract explicitly: reply-required versus fire-and-forget, where the reply goes, and which exception maps to the error channel.
Acknowledge after the service has completed, never on receipt; a message whose service call threw must end up unacknowledged, retried or on the invalid-message channel.
Make the endpoint safe under at-least-once delivery: deduplicate by message id, or make the service idempotent.
Bound concurrency deliberately (competing consumers, worker pool) and apply backpressure to the input channel instead of spawning unbounded tasks.
Declare one endpoint per (channel, service method) pair and keep the mapping declarative so it can be reviewed.
Test the service as a plain unit and the endpoint with a test message injected into the channel - no broker required.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Service Activator (Message Endpoints chapter).
